paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions in which a learner chooses several options, called arms, at once. Ordinary semi-bandit feedback reveals the rewards of the selected arms. Here, a graph adds information: selecting an arm also reveals rewards for its neighbors. The question is how this extra visibility changes the difficulty of learning.

The authors establish an optimal regret rate of S√T + √(αST), up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures the learner’s accumulated shortfall relative to the best fixed decision. Here, S is the number of selected arms, T is the time horizon, and α is the graph’s independence number. The result connects the known full-information and ordinary semi-bandit rates.

A crucial ingredient is how a fractional decision becomes an actual random selection: the selected components must have suitable negative correlations. The authors show that merely matching the fractional action in expectation within online stochastic mirror descent is suboptimal. They also derive an improved regret upper bound for a general-capacity version of the problem.
icml-2025-adversarial-combinatorial-semi.tldr: The paper establishes optimal regret for combinatorial semi-bandits with graph feedback and shows why correlations in randomized decisions matter.

paragraphs: Large language models require substantial storage and computation because they contain so many parameters. Pruning reduces this burden by removing parameters, but choosing what to remove presents an optimization problem. The paper targets a gap between expensive methods involving retraining and one-shot heuristics that lack theoretical guarantees about their behavior.

The authors formulate pruning as an optimization problem with an ℓ0 penalty, which penalizes the number of retained nonzero parameters. They propose monotone accelerated Iterative Hard Thresholding, or mAIHT, to solve this formulation. This makes the preference for a smaller model an explicit part of the objective rather than leaving parameter removal entirely to a heuristic rule.

The theoretical analysis addresses whether the method converges, how quickly it converges, and upper bounds on risk. Experiments pruning LLaMA-7B report better performance than state-of-the-art pruning techniques across several evaluation metrics. The contribution therefore combines an analyzed optimization procedure with empirical evidence on a specific language model, supporting a more principled approach to reducing model size.
icml-2025-an-efficient-pruner-for-large-.tldr: mAIHT casts language-model pruning as sparse optimization, combining convergence and risk analysis with improved pruning results on LLaMA-7B.

paragraphs: Watermarking generated text aims to make its origin detectable by deliberately influencing generation. Existing methods can lose effectiveness after text is modified, while the changes used to insert a watermark may also harm output quality. This paper addresses the tradeoff between making a watermark survive editing and preserving useful language-model behavior.

The proposed method perturbs logits, the scores a model assigns to possible next tokens. It jointly optimizes the watermark encoder and decoder so that inserting and recognizing the watermark are trained together. Because some operations in this pipeline are not differentiable, an online-prompting technique uses the on-the-fly language model as a differentiable surrogate.

The authors report robustness improvements over distortion-free methods of 37–39% under paraphrasing and 17.2% on average. Text quality remains comparable to those methods according to perplexity and downstream-task evaluations. These findings support joint optimization as a way to improve the quality–robustness balance. The abstract also states that the approach can be generalized to different language models.
icml-2025-an-end-to-end-model-for-logits.tldr: Jointly training watermark insertion and detection improves robustness to text changes while maintaining comparable measured text quality.

paragraphs: Methods for controlling language models include prompting, finetuning, and interventions in their internal representations. Comparing them has been difficult without a shared evaluation. AxBench supplies a large-scale benchmark covering two distinct abilities: steering generated text toward a desired concept and detecting whether a concept is present in a model’s representations.

Experiments on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B reveal different winners for the two tasks. Prompting performs best for steering among the existing methods evaluated, followed by finetuning. Representation-based approaches, including difference-in-means, perform best at concept detection. Sparse autoencoders are not competitive on either evaluation, showing that their appeal for interpretability does not translate into leading results on these tests.

The authors also introduce Rank-1 Representation Finetuning, called ReFT-r1, a weakly supervised method that is competitive on both tasks while offering interpretability advantages absent from prompting. They release feature dictionaries at sparse-autoencoder scale for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean. The results make the intended use central: recognizing concepts and controlling outputs call for separate comparisons.
icml-2025-axbench-steering-llms-even-sim.tldr: AxBench finds prompting strongest for steering and representation methods strongest for concept detection, with sparse autoencoders uncompetitive on both evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: In overparameterized logistic regression, gradient descent can keep increasing the size of its parameter vector while its direction approaches the maximum ℓ2-margin solution. This paper asks whether stopping earlier provides statistical benefits beyond that limiting directional behavior. Its analysis concerns a well-specified, high-dimensional logistic-regression setting, making the modeling assumptions central to the conclusions.

The authors show that excess logistic risk vanishes for early-stopped gradient descent but grows without bound for the iterates as training approaches its limit. They interpret this as suggesting good calibration for early stopping and statistical inconsistency for asymptotic gradient descent. Thus, the eventual direction of the parameters does not by itself establish good probability predictions.

For classification error, they establish another separation: polynomially many samples suffice for early stopping to achieve small excess zero-one risk, whereas any interpolating estimator requires exponentially many in the analyzed setting. Finally, finite-sample bounds compare the norm and angle of early-stopped solutions with explicitly ℓ2-regularized solutions, connecting stopping time to regularization.
icml-2025-benefits-of-early-stopping-in-.tldr: Under well-specified high-dimensional logistic regression, early stopping yields strong risk and sample-efficiency benefits over training toward an interpolating limit.

paragraphs: Embedding-based systems need representations that balance useful information against storage and computation. Matryoshka Representation Learning addresses this through adjustable embedding lengths, but the abstract identifies full model retraining and reduced performance at short lengths as drawbacks. This paper investigates sparse coding as another way to make representations adapt to different computational budgets.

Contrastive Sparse Representation, or CSR, maps pretrained embeddings into a larger feature space in which only selected features are active. A lightweight autoencoder and task-aware contrastive objectives aim to retain semantic information. Adaptation comes from changing the level of sparsity, allowing inference to use different amounts of active information without requiring the same approach as shortening a dense embedding.

Across image, text, and multimodal benchmarks, CSR consistently outperforms Matryoshka Representation Learning in accuracy and retrieval speed, often substantially, while taking a fraction of its training time. These results support sparse representations as a practical alternative for the tested settings. The central finding is that a high-dimensional representation can still support efficient inference when its activity is selective.
icml-2025-beyond-matryoshka-revisiting-s.tldr: CSR converts pretrained embeddings into selectively active features, improving accuracy, retrieval speed, and training efficiency over Matryoshka learning in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies protecting predictions by adding noise to the outputs of a model trained without privacy protection. How much noise is needed depends on prediction sensitivity: how much a prediction could change when the training data change. Existing approaches use global sensitivity, which can lead to unfavorable privacy–utility tradeoffs compared with private training.

The authors develop dataset-specific upper bounds on prediction sensitivity using convex relaxation and bound propagation. Rather than relying only on a global bound, their analysis accounts for the particular dataset. They then combine these bounds with the smooth sensitivity mechanism, providing the privacy machinery needed to use this more tailored sensitivity information.

Experiments on real-world medical image classification and natural-language-processing datasets show that the resulting bounds can be orders of magnitude tighter than global-sensitivity bounds. The reported advance is therefore a substantially sharper analysis of private prediction. It supports improving the amount of noise justified by sensitivity analysis, while the stated empirical comparison concerns bound tightness rather than a universal advantage over private training.
icml-2025-certification-for-differential.tldr: Dataset-specific sensitivity bounds combined with smooth sensitivity sharpen privacy analysis for noisy predictions from non-private models.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce representations that group semantically related examples despite receiving no class labels. This paper investigates how those clustering properties differ across components of joint embedding architectures. Using several metrics, the authors find that the encoder’s output has stronger and more stable clustering properties than the other components they examine.

They use that observation to develop Representation Self-Assignment, or ReSA. The method turns the model’s existing tendency to form clusters into guidance for further learning. Its positive-feedback design aims to strengthen useful representational structure through the structure already emerging in the model, making clustering an active learning resource rather than only a property measured after training.

On standard self-supervised-learning benchmarks, models pretrained with ReSA outperform other state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Further analysis reports improved clustering at both fine and coarse levels, meaning the benefits extend across different levels of grouping. Together, the findings connect where useful structure appears inside the architecture with a method for improving that structure during training.
icml-2025-clustering-properties-of-self-.tldr: ReSA uses the encoder’s strong clustering structure to guide self-supervised learning, improving benchmark performance and clustering at multiple levels.

paragraphs: Historical numbers do not always contain all the information needed for a forecast. Background knowledge and constraints may instead be expressed in language. Context is Key, or CiK, tests whether forecasting systems can combine numerical time series with this additional information, addressing an unresolved question about the capabilities of language-model-based forecasters.

The benchmark pairs numerical data with varied, carefully constructed textual context. Every task requires understanding that text to succeed, so contextual reasoning is part of the task’s design rather than an optional source of help. This gives the evaluation a specific purpose: measuring whether models can use information that the numerical history alone does not adequately communicate.

The authors compare statistical methods, time-series foundation models, and language-model-based forecasters. They also propose a simple prompting method that outperforms all other approaches tested on CiK. The experiments show promising language-model forecasting performance alongside critical shortcomings. These findings motivate evaluation and development of systems that combine both modalities while remaining accessible to decision-makers with different levels of technical expertise.
icml-2025-context-is-key-a-benchmark-for.tldr: CiK evaluates forecasts that require textual context, finding a simple LLM prompting method strongest among the tested approaches.

paragraphs: DiffusionVLA combines language-based reasoning with diffusion-based robot action generation. A pretrained vision-language model decomposes and explains tasks, while a diffusion policy produces actions. The framework addresses the complementary weaknesses identified in the abstract: limited action precision and robustness in autoregressive vision-language-action models, and missing reasoning capabilities in diffusion policies.

A reasoning injection module places the model’s own reasoning phrases directly into policy learning. This connects its explanations to action generation and supports visualizing the decision process for failure diagnosis. Experiments across multiple real robots include factory sorting with objects absent from training and zero-shot bin picking, where the model reaches 63.7% accuracy on 102 previously unseen objects.

The reported tests also show robustness to distractors and new backgrounds, adaptation to different robot embodiments, and the ability to follow novel instructions while retaining conversation. The smallest, 2-billion-parameter model runs at 82 Hz on one A6000 GPU. Scaling from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters improves generalization in the authors’ experiments, alongside reported data efficiency.
icml-2025-diffusionvla-scaling-robot-fou.tldr: DiffusionVLA injects language-model reasoning into diffusion policies, enabling fast robot control and improved generalization in real-robot experiments.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction uses held-out calibration data to turn model outputs into prediction sets with statistical coverage guarantees. This paper considers a decentralized setting where individual devices have little calibration data and can communicate only with neighboring devices. The challenge is to support reliable prediction through local exchanges over a graph rather than centralized calibration.

The authors propose two message-passing methods. Quantile-based distributed conformal prediction, Q-DCP, uses distributed quantile regression, with tailored smoothing and regularization to accelerate convergence. Histogram-based distributed conformal prediction, H-DCP, instead uses consensus to estimate a histogram. These approaches offer different ways for devices to collectively obtain the information needed for calibration.

Experiments examine their behavior across network topologies, comparing tuning requirements, communication costs, coverage guarantees, and prediction-set sizes. These dimensions matter together: a method’s calibration behavior must be considered alongside the exchanges and tuning it requires. The paper’s contribution is a pair of decentralized approaches and an investigation of their tradeoffs, rather than a stated single winner for every network.
icml-2025-distributed-conformal-predicti.tldr: Two message-passing methods enable decentralized conformal calibration while exposing tradeoffs among communication, tuning, coverage, and prediction-set size.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects becomes difficult when collecting post-treatment outcomes is expensive. The paper gives imaging and biopsy procedures as examples of costly labeling. It asks how active learning can choose useful additional observations within a limited budget, improving estimation through targeted data acquisition rather than relying only on a more complex estimator.

The theoretical analysis identifies factual and counterfactual covering radii as quantities determining an upper bound on risk. These describe coverage relevant to observed treatment outcomes and alternative-treatment comparisons. The authors first propose a greedy algorithm that reduces these radii. Its strength is established under an idealized, balanced data distribution, making that condition important to the method’s stated effectiveness.

To handle more realistic distributions, they introduce FCCM, which reformulates acquisition as maximizing factual and counterfactual coverage. This objective is designed to achieve effective radius reduction as new labels are acquired. Comparisons against other methods on fully synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets favor FCCM. The results connect a theoretically motivated coverage objective to empirical improvements in budget-constrained treatment-effect estimation.
icml-2025-enhancing-treatment-effect-est.tldr: FCCM selects treatment-outcome labels by improving factual and counterfactual coverage, outperforming compared methods on synthetic and semi-synthetic data.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models learn internal representations from sequential data, but what these representations contain remains poorly understood. This paper examines both their organization and their learned concepts. It compares the similarity of layer representations within models and across model sizes, bringing representational analysis used in language and vision to time-series models.

The analysis finds redundancy arranged in blocks: groups of representations exhibit substantial similarity. The authors show that this structure can inform pruning to improve inference speed and efficiency. The practical connection is that inspecting internal similarity can guide decisions about reducing computation, making representational analysis useful for model simplification as well as understanding.

The paper also investigates concepts such as periodicity and trends. It demonstrates that conceptual priors can be extracted from model representations and used to steer outputs toward predictions informed by those concepts. These two directions give the analysis complementary purposes: identifying redundant computation and exposing meaningful structure that can influence forecasts. Together, they offer methods for making time-series foundation models more efficient and transparent.
icml-2025-exploring-representations-and-.tldr: Analyzing time-series model representations reveals redundancy useful for pruning and learned concepts that can guide prediction steering.

paragraphs: Multi-view classification uses different forms of information about the same examples, such as multiple feature sets, sequences, or modalities. This paper tackles the harder setting where some views and some labels are missing. The central challenge is learning representations that distinguish classes despite having incomplete inputs and limited supervision.

The authors start from the sufficiency of shared information across views for downstream tasks. They argue that existing contrastive approaches to missing-view data have limited ability to learn consistent representations. Their method pursues greater mutual information across views while aiming to reduce redundant information unrelated to the task, concentrating representation learning on useful shared semantics.

To address missing labels, the method adds a two-branch strategy that uses soft pseudo-labels for cross-imputation. This supplies estimated label information within the learning process alongside the shared-representation objective. Experiments on multiple benchmarks report advantages over compared methods and compatibility with both incomplete and complete data. The contribution combines handling missing input views with handling missing supervision, treating both as obstacles to learning discriminative representations.
icml-2025-learning-compact-semantic-info.tldr: The method combines shared-information learning across views with soft pseudo-label cross-imputation to improve classification when inputs and labels are incomplete.

paragraphs: Pretraining for reinforcement learning must prepare an agent to discover solutions through interaction, rather than simply imitate labeled examples. This paper investigates how unlabeled recordings of prior behavior can improve that exploration. It combines two uses of prior data: extracting reusable low-level skills and supplying additional experience to an online learning algorithm.

SUPE first learns low-level skills with a variational autoencoder. It then assigns optimistic reward estimates and high-level action labels to the unlabeled trajectories. These pseudo-labels transform existing recordings into examples that can train decisions over skills and encourage novelty-seeking behavior. The prior data therefore contribute both the building blocks of behavior and guidance for using them.

During online reinforcement learning, a high-level policy learns to compose the pretrained skills, using the transformed trajectories as additional off-policy data. Across 42 long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards, SUPE consistently outperforms earlier strategies in the reported experiments. The findings support the authors’ claim that carefully combining skill pretraining with reuse of prior experience can compound their exploration benefits.
icml-2025-leveraging-skills-from-unlabel.tldr: SUPE turns unlabeled trajectories into reusable skills and exploration-oriented training examples, improving results across 42 sparse-reward tasks.

paragraphs: Web-scale pretraining datasets contain enormous amounts of text, but their unstructured organization makes systematic curation difficult. WebOrganizer addresses this by classifying pages along two complementary dimensions: what they discuss and the format in which they present it. These categories make the composition of a large corpus easier to examine and deliberately adjust.

The framework distills annotations from a large language model into efficient classifiers that automatically label pretraining data. With those labels, the authors study how mixing different domains affects downstream performance. They find that combining insights about useful topics with insights about useful formats produces further gains, making both dimensions relevant to data selection.

Domain mixing also improves existing quality-based selection methods in the reported study. The authors additionally examine how quality filters implicitly alter the mixture of domains, connecting quality judgments to corpus composition. The findings support domain organization as a complement to quality filtering: it provides explicit categories for understanding and adjusting what a model encounters during pretraining.
icml-2025-organize-the-web-constructing-.tldr: WebOrganizer labels web data by topic and format, enabling domain mixtures that improve pretraining and complement quality-based filtering.

paragraphs: Predicting how cellular gene expression responds to perturbations could help researchers study cell processes and disease mechanisms computationally. PertEval-scFM provides a standardized framework for evaluating models on this task. Its central question is whether representations from single-cell foundation models improve prediction of these responses compared with simpler baseline models.

The evaluation specifically examines foundation-model embeddings used in a zero-shot setting. These embeddings provide contextualized representations, but the benchmark asks whether that representation translates into useful predictive gains. The authors find only limited improvement over simple baselines, with the problem particularly apparent under distribution shift, when the prediction setting differs from the data conditions supporting the model.

The result identifies a task-specific limitation of the evaluated zero-shot embeddings rather than establishing that every use of single-cell foundation models is ineffective. The authors argue for specialized models and higher-quality datasets covering a broader range of cellular states. Their contribution is both an evaluation framework and evidence that broad pretraining alone has not resolved perturbation-effect prediction in this setting.
icml-2025-perteval-scfm-benchmarking-sin.tldr: PertEval-scFM finds limited gains from zero-shot single-cell foundation-model embeddings for perturbation prediction, especially under distribution shift.

paragraphs: A useful confidence estimate should help identify likely mistakes and express uncertainty accurately. These goals can come apart: the abstract notes that methods improving calibration may harm failure prediction. This paper compares information-theoretic confidence measures that can be applied after training, without changing a neural network’s architecture or its training procedure.

The study examines pointwise mutual information, pointwise V-information, and pointwise sliced mutual information, abbreviated PMI, PVI, and PSI. Its theoretical discussion connects them to predictive uncertainty through properties including invariance, convergence rates, and sensitivity to geometric features such as margin and intrinsic dimensionality. This provides a basis for comparing how the measures behave beyond their empirical scores.

Across benchmark computer-vision models and datasets, PVI consistently beats PMI, PSI, and existing post-hoc baselines for failure prediction across metrics. For calibration, it matches temperature-scaled softmax, a strong baseline. The reported result is therefore a favorable combination: improved identification of errors alongside competitive calibration. The authors connect this balance to the tradeoffs suggested by their theoretical analysis.
icml-2025-pointwise-information-measures.tldr: PVI improves failure prediction over compared confidence estimators while matching temperature-scaled softmax calibration in computer-vision experiments.

paragraphs: Protein models often benefit from retrieving homologs, sequences related to the protein being studied. Traditional workflows retrieve these through multiple sequence alignments before training a downstream model. The abstract identifies three problems with that separation: expensive retrieval, difficulties with highly divergent sequences or complex insertions and deletions, and retrieval that is disconnected from the final task.

Protriever makes retrieval and task learning part of one differentiable framework. It learns which homologs are relevant while simultaneously training for the target objective. Efficient vector search replaces the alignment-centered retrieval approach, tying the selection of supporting sequences more directly to what the downstream model needs to predict.

For protein fitness prediction, the authors report state-of-the-art performance relative to sequence-based models using alignment-based homolog retrieval, together with a two-orders-of-magnitude speed advantage. They describe the framework as independent of a particular architecture or task and adaptable to different databases and retrieval strategies at inference time. The demonstrated fitness results support its promise as a scalable alternative to the conventional two-stage workflow.
icml-2025-protriever-end-to-end-differen.tldr: Protriever jointly learns protein-homolog retrieval and fitness prediction, reporting stronger performance and roughly 100-fold greater speed than the specified alignment-based comparison.

paragraphs: RE-Bench evaluates language-model agents on open-ended machine-learning research engineering and compares them directly with human experts. It contains seven challenging environments and records 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 experts. The benchmark addresses a gap in realistic evaluations of AI research-and-development capabilities, which are relevant to anticipating increasing automation.

The human results show that the environments allow meaningful progress: 82% of expert attempts receive a nonzero score, and 24% match or exceed strong reference solutions. The authors compare these results with public frontier models using different agent designs, time budgets, and best-of-k selection, which evaluates the best result among multiple attempts.

The ranking changes with available time. At a total budget of two hours per environment, the best agents score four times as highly as human experts. Humans benefit more from additional time, narrowly leading at eight hours and reaching twice the top agent’s score at 32 total hours across attempts. These findings make time budget and attempt allocation essential to interpreting the comparison.
icml-2025-re-bench-evaluating-frontier-a.tldr: RE-Bench finds top AI agents ahead at short research-engineering time budgets, while human experts gain more from additional time.

paragraphs: Fixed-backbone protein design chooses amino-acid sequences for a specified backbone structure. Leading methods discussed in the abstract do not explicitly model sidechain conformations during sequence generation, despite their importance to protein stability and function. FAMPNN addresses this gap by representing both the amino-acid identity and the three-dimensional sidechain conformation of each residue.

These two outputs have different forms: amino-acid identity is discrete, while sidechain conformation is continuous. FAMPNN learns their distributions jointly using categorical cross-entropy together with a diffusion loss. This allows sequence design and sidechain modeling to participate in the same learning task, explicitly incorporating structural information that other approaches must infer from backbone geometry and sequence.

The authors find that joint learning benefits both tasks, improving sequence recovery while achieving state-of-the-art sidechain packing. They also report benefits for zero-shot prediction of experimental binding and stability measurements. The evidence therefore extends beyond reconstructing sequences to practical prediction tasks, supporting the usefulness of explicitly modeling full-atom structure during protein sequence design.
icml-2025-sidechain-conditioning-and-mod.tldr: FAMPNN jointly models amino-acid identity and sidechain geometry, improving sequence recovery, sidechain packing, and zero-shot binding and stability prediction.

paragraphs: Spatial Reasoning Models, or SRMs, use denoising generative models to reason about sets of continuous variables. Given observations for some variables, they infer representations for the remaining ones. The paper focuses on the difficulty of doing this reliably for complex distributions, where spatial generative models can produce hallucinated outputs.

The authors introduce benchmark tasks designed to measure complex reasoning and quantify hallucination. Within the SRM framework, they investigate sequential generation, the order in which variables are generated, and sampling strategies during training. This treats the generation procedure as an important part of reasoning performance, alongside the model’s ability to represent the underlying variables.

A central finding is that the denoising network itself can successfully predict the order of generation, which the authors describe as a first demonstration. Using the resulting insights raises accuracy on specific reasoning tasks from below 1% to above 50%. The gains are stated for those tasks, showing that generation order and training choices can materially affect reasoning in this framework.
icml-2025-spatial-reasoning-with-denoisi.tldr: SRMs show that generation order and training choices can sharply improve continuous-variable reasoning, with denoising networks learning to predict generation order.

paragraphs: Understanding why language models refuse requests requires examining how refusal is represented internally. Earlier work suggested that a single direction in activation space determines this behavior. This paper develops a gradient-based representation-engineering approach and uses it to investigate whether refusal instead involves a richer collection of internal structures.

The authors identify multiple independent refusal directions as well as multidimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. They also show that orthogonality, meaning directions are geometrically perpendicular, does not establish independence when those directions are manipulated. This distinction matters because a geometric relationship between representations does not fully describe how interventions affect the model’s behavior.

To address that gap, the paper introduces representational independence, accounting for both linear and nonlinear effects. Using this framework, it identifies mechanistically independent refusal directions and concludes that multiple distinct mechanisms contribute to refusal in the studied models. The contribution is therefore both a more complex account of refusal geometry and a method for examining functional independence, with potential use in further research on language-model internals.
icml-2025-the-geometry-of-refusal-in-lar.tldr: Refusal involves multiple independent directions and concept cones, and geometric orthogonality alone does not establish independence under intervention.

paragraphs: Controlling a language model often requires considering properties of the whole continuation, such as toxicity or personalization. Next-token prediction does not directly provide that lookahead. TRACE addresses this by estimating how likely future text is to satisfy a desired attribute, avoiding repeated post-training for each attribute or expensive sampling-based estimates.

The framework distills a Hidden Markov Model from the language model and combines it with a small attribute classifier. It then computes Expected Attribute Probability exactly over the distilled model’s predicted futures. This exactness applies to the HMM calculation. TRACE uses the result to reweight the original language model’s next-token probabilities, bringing information about possible continuations into each generation step.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art detoxification with 20% decoding overhead. TRACE also produces 76 low-resource personalized language models within seconds and extends to combinations of attributes. These findings support using a tractable probabilistic model as a lightweight control component, allowing attribute adaptation while retaining the original language model as the generator.
icml-2025-trace-back-from-the-future-a-p.tldr: TRACE uses exact lookahead over a distilled Hidden Markov Model to guide language generation toward desired attributes with modest reported overhead.

paragraphs: Switchback experiments evaluate policies by switching between them over time. Their design must account for the fact that a policy’s effects may persist after a switch and that reward errors may be related across time. This paper compares switchback designs in Markovian environments, examining how these two features shape their effectiveness.

The analysis covers a range of state-of-the-art estimators from reinforcement learning. That scope extends beyond selecting an optimal design for one relatively simple estimator. The authors find that design effectiveness depends crucially on the magnitude of carryover effects and on reward-error autocorrelation. Both the persistence of treatment effects and the temporal pattern of errors therefore matter to the comparison.

The findings apply across all the estimators considered in the paper, which is the stated meaning of estimator-agnostic here. Using these insights, the authors provide a workflow to guide practitioners designing switchback A/B tests. The contribution connects properties of the experimental environment to design decisions while retaining relevance across several estimation methods.
icml-2025-unraveling-the-interplay-betwe.tldr: Switchback design effectiveness depends on carryover and reward-error autocorrelation, with findings that hold across the reinforcement-learning estimators analyzed.
